Explore the life and works of famed polish composer Frédéric Chopin in this clip from the first episode of Now Hear This Season 6, Now Hear This "Chopin's Polish Heart." About NOW HEAR THIS Season 6: Scott Yoo, conductor and artistic director of the Mexico City Philharmonic, returns with the sixth season of the critically acclaimed series NOW HEAR THIS to examine the musical inspirations of Frédéric Chopin, Luigi Boccherini, Sergei Rachmaninoff and Agustín Barrios. Advertisement Become a KPBS sponsor Journey to Poland to understand Chopin's Polish heart, head to Spain to enjoy Boccherini's night music, explore the legacy of Rachmaninoff and then learn how Barrios emerged as the greatest guitar composer of the 20th century. All these composers are expats or exiles, their music shaped by nostalgia for a homeland they couldn’t return to, and new friendships, ideas and opportunities in new places. Their careers were marked by loss and longing, but ultimately renewal and redemption. Arcos Film + Music LLC / PBS Pianist Jan Lisiecki and host Scott Yoo. Yoo visits Poland, Paraguay, Uruguay, Brazil, France, Switzerland, Mexico and more to explore the the musical evolution of these artists and play the compositions that solidified their musical legacy. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-andy-.text: LONDON — As Britain’s children head back to school, its new prime minister needs to decide exactly how he wants to keep them off social media. Britain isn’t the only country crafting a social media ban for minors. Developments in Australia and France over the break should give Burnham’s ministers and officials plenty to think about. Australia’s ban is only having a limited effect on how much kids get on to social media, while France’s ban has hit a huge legal hurdle. In June, then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced plans to ban social media for under-16s — only to resign a week later and leave his successor Andy Burnham with an in-tray of unanswered questions about a policy that upends the U.K.’s current online safety regime. Advertisement Advertisement MPs return to Parliament next week after the summer break, and Burnham’s government will need to decide how the ban — which is supposed to come into effect in spring — will work. Australia Australia was the first country in the world to introduce a social media ban for kids in December last year. Last month, the Australian government published its first wave of findings on the experiences of more than 4,000 children and families since the ban took effect. The numbers do not show a huge drop in kids accessing social media. The proportion of under-16s holding at least one social media account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.3 percent at the three-month follow-up. Meanwhile, the proportion who reported using a social media platform (with or without an account) fell even less, from 85.9 percent to 81.5 percent. Australia only requires age-restricted platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from creating or keeping accounts. Access via logged-out experiences, for example, is permissible. The rationale is that account-based access — and the data harvesting that comes with it — increases the likelihood of exposure to potentially harmful design features, such as algorithmic suggestions or infinite scroll. But the U.K. could go further than Australia by casting a wider net to cover both account ownership and access. That could implicate not just the social media platforms, but internet service providers too. The previous Starmer government has already laid the groundwork by handing itself powers , via the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, to force ISPs to keep kids out. Advertisement Advertisement France France was eager to pursue its own ban for under-15s, but earlier this month the country’s Constitutional Council blocked President Emmanuel Macron’s proposed social media ban , arguing the legislation would disproportionately violate children’s rights to privacy, freedom of expression, and communication. While the U.K.’s unwritten constitution means there’s no equivalent judicial mechanism here — the Supreme Court has no power to strike down laws — the ruling across the Channel serves as a reminder that sweeping proposals can easily get gummed up in the courts. The U.K. looks set to rely on secondary legislation to push through the ban, meaning the government can largely bypass parliamentary debate. Starmer said the reason for this was to fast-track the ban. “We’ve taken the powers to make sure we can act within months, not years,” he said. Secondary legislation may allow the government to move faster, but it is particularly vulnerable to judicial review, and could invite an unlikely coalition of tech companies and digital rights activists to challenge restrictions via this route. “The inevitable consequence of such broad regulatory discretion is an explosion in litigation,” Oliver Carroll, legal director at law firm Bird & Bird, previously told POLITICO .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj75.text: Image source, BBC/Getty Images Image caption, Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow By Liza Fokht Senior reporter, BBC News Russian Published 3 hours ago "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year. The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials. Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed. Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia. "There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty." The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023 Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater. "Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow. Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission. The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution". Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials. One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy. Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia Published 4 days ago Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Published 4 September They fled Russia, but the West sent them back Published 6 days ago Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police. One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear. Not everyone can deal with the pressure. One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months. 'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats' In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy. He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be. The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible. And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies. Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country. But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024 After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers. One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'." Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses. A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase. "It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage". Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies. This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs." Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level." But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow. "Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters." Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm. But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians. "Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqy7lv.text: Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Close Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology. https://www.politico.eu/article/big-oil-.text: BRUSSELS — The European Commission is preparing to delay a key EU climate law by a year, as a concession to the fossil fuel sector, the Trump administration and some EU member countries. But already Big Oil is pushing for more drastic changes to the landmark Methane Regulation , and supporters of the law fear it will be hard to stop them from getting their way. The EU executive is expected on Wednesday to outline plans to postpone rules that would force oil and gas companies to report methane emissions, a potent greenhouse gas and a major driver of climate change. The rules were originally due to come into effect in January. Advertisement Advertisement The move follows warnings from the sector, backed by the U.S.government and several member countries , including France, that the rules remained unclear and would deter exporters from selling to Europe, risking supply disruptions at a time when Europe already faces a winter crunch . But industry is already signaling it won't accept the Commission's concession. On Friday, the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers, the industry's top Brussels lobby group, reiterated its longstanding call for a three-year delay, arguing the proposal "was insufficient to fully mitigate these risks and would leave the EU facing the same implementation challenges in 12 months' time." Some member countries are likely to follow suit when they raise the issue at a summit of European leaders on Friday, as well as at a gathering of deputy ambassadors on October 28. EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen said in Dublin last month that any delay would be conditional on countries implementing the rules at the local level, as only a smattering have done so far. He added at a parliamentary hearing in Strasbourg last week that lawmakers shouldn't try to amend the proposal to add further delays. But defenders of the rules acknowledge that this will be difficult in practice, given the diminishing influence of green-minded lawmakers in the European Parliament and growing political sensitivities around high energy costs linked to the Iran war. "If Trump pushes prices higher and higher, it will be easier to achieve" further concessions, said one EU official, granted anonymity to discuss the rule change candidly. Advertisement Advertisement The EU lawmaking process could also work against the Commission's aims, with critics arguing that reopening the rules invariably leaves them exposed to meddling. While the executive drafts the proposal, lawmakers and member countries can push for their own revisions . If the Commission were to reopen the methane regulation, "the first thing that would happen is that in the Parliament, a rejection amendment would be taken up, saying, ‘OK, let’s do away with the whole methane regulation,’ and I believe it would find a majority,” Jutta Paulus, a German lawmaker with the Greens who negotiated the file on behalf of the Parliament ahead of its adoption, told POLITICO before the summer. The Commission would have limited tools to ensure the revision doesn’t go beyond the targeted changes, she added. However, they could draw on historical precedents, she said, recalling that the Commission threatened to withdraw rules updating the legal status of wolves in 2015 if lawmakers went too far. That's exactly what a group of center-left European lawmakers called for in a letter sent Monday to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and senior commissioners. The letter, seen by POLITICO, called on the Commission to "make full use of its right to withdraw the proposal" if lawmakers try to add further amendments, adding that the proposal should include a "binding implementation roadmap." MEPs and some national officials have already signaled that they will indeed push for more. The proposal is "not sufficient," Czech Trade Minister Karel Havlicek, who engineered the member country campaign to delay the rules, told POLITICO. But he added that "the whole legislative process is ahead of us." Prominent center-right MEP Christian Ehler called for a three-year delay last week. Diplomats also say some member countries hope the Commission will use a review of the rules scheduled for January 2028 to explore whether further postponements are possible. But that remains speculative, and for now the one-year delay will include only timeline updates, with no conditions attached or provisions for further delay, despite Commissioner Jørgensen's hints to the contrary, three people briefed on the matter said. A Commission spokesperson declined to comment. Advertisement Advertisement Germany, which is divided on the rules, supports a year-long delay but has yet to signal support for a longer one, said one person familiar with the country's position. The current iteration of the rules, adopted in 2024, was itself born of 11th-hour institutional horse-trading over which the Commission had limited influence. The regulation was originally designed to target domestic producers, and the obligations on imports were a parliamentary concession agreed in last-minute negotiations between lawmakers and governments, said Paulus, the lead negotiator. Bargains had to be struck at the last minute, she added, recalling that she was able to convince Polish MEPs in the far-right European Conservatives and Reformists grouping to accept the rules only by persuading them that the reporting requirements would be useful in "drying out" Russian shadow fleet operations. The EU had no ban on Russian gas at the time. Another question is whether member countries will agree to develop the rules at the local level. While member countries have complained that the rules are unclear on which third-party tools firms can use to demonstrate the reliability of their reporting on emissions, the legislation itself says it is primarily up to governments to figure this out. “The rules say implementation is down to member states even when the [regulation] leaves spaces for filling the blanks — the flexibility is the whole point,” said Léa Pilsner, the director of energy policy at Environmental Defense Fund Europe. At the same time, even some national officials from countries that have implemented the rules have argued that they still need more guidance from the Commission. Advertisement Advertisement
